prompt: Which question does an operational screen exist to answer?
hint: Think of Marcos at 11:00 with fourteen trucks out.

choices.text: Are we on plan this month, and where should the budget move?
choices.why: That is the tactical question of lesson 15, asked by managers over weeks.

choices.text: What needs my attention now?
choices.why: Right: decisions in minutes, by people on the floor, about the rows that are wrong.

choices.text: Is the company heading the right way over the years?
choices.why: That is the strategic question of lesson 16, for the owners and the board.

choices.text: Why were deliveries late across the whole month?
choices.why: A why across a month is diagnostic analysis (lesson 7), asked at the monthly review.

prompt: At 11:00 the fourteen routes were 19.3 minutes behind on average. Why is that a poor headline for Marcos's screen?
hint: One route was 74 minutes behind.

choices.text: The median of 13.5 is the correct summary of delays, and the mean is not
choices.why: The median hides route 11 just as well; any single summary points at no truck.

choices.text: Averages of delays need a full day of data behind them before they settle into anything useful
choices.why: The figure is correct for 11:00; the problem is what it hides, not when it was taken.

choices.text: It hides the one route far behind among thirteen that need nothing
choices.why: Right: Marcos needs the row that is wrong, and the average dissolves it.

choices.text: The routes on time pull it up, so it overstates the delays
choices.why: Routes at zero pull an average down, not up.

prompt: Match each person and moment at Varanda with the screen that serves the decision.
hint: The question decides the screen, and so does the horizon.

pairs.right: The routes 30 or more minutes behind, most behind first
The products missing from the shelf right now
Spend and orders by channel against the target
Five numbers over five years, against plan

right_distractors: A pie of the month's deliveries by region

prompt: Lesson 9 handed reorders to an automatic rule. Why does a person, and not a rule, decide to move stops between trucks?
hint: What does the decision depend on that the data does not hold?

choices.text: Moving a delivery is rare and expensive, so it needs a director's signature
choices.why: It is frequent and cheap to undo; that is not why a person decides.

choices.text: It turns on facts outside the data, such as whether the customer will take it later
choices.why: Right: the customer and the second driver are not in the data, so the screen suggests and Marcos decides.

choices.text: The delivery data arrives once a month, too late for a rule
choices.why: They are copied every ten minutes; lateness is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Personal-data law forbids an automatic rule from changing anything in a customer's order without consent
choices.why: The lesson cites no such rule; the reason is what the decision depends on.

prompt: Why do the tiles at the top of Marcos's board show counts (4 late, 57 at risk) and not percentages?
hint: What does Marcos act on?

choices.text: Counts have no decimals, so they are more precise than rates
choices.why: Precision is not the point; a rate can be exact and still hide four waiting customers.

choices.text: A percentage would need the whole month of data
choices.why: Today's 4 out of 286 is a rate for today; no month is needed.

choices.text: Four late out of 286, as a rate, is a decimal near 100 that reads as good news
choices.why: Right: the count names what he has to act on; the rate turns it into reassurance.

choices.text: Rates are for the board of directors and counts are for the staff on the floor, by long convention
choices.why: There is no such convention; the choice follows the decision the screen serves.

prompt: The eleven routes needing no action stay on the board as small chips. What would go wrong if they were removed?
hint: A route can also vanish because its data stops.

choices.text: A route whose phone stopped sending would look like one with no problem
choices.why: Right: with every route shown, a missing one is visible instead of silent.

choices.text: Marcos could no longer compare this month's routes with the same routes last month
choices.why: The chips show today's minutes behind; month comparisons belong to lesson 15.

choices.text: The board would break the design rule that a screen shows each row of the data it receives
choices.why: There is no such rule; the exceptions list itself leaves rows out on purpose.

choices.text: The space would be taken by a monthly chart
choices.why: Space is not the argument; the chips are there so a missing route can be noticed.

prompt: Which of these belong on Marcos's delivery board? Choose all that apply.
hint: Keep what changes what he does before lunch.

choices.text: The time the data describes, and how old it is
choices.why: Right: without it a frozen board looks current.

choices.text: The weekly on-time rate for the quarter, as a line
choices.why: A trend over weeks answers Caio's question at the monthly review, not Marcos's.

choices.text: The routes 30 or more minutes behind, each with a next step
choices.why: Right: the exceptions, sorted, with what to do.

choices.text: How many orders have already missed their window
choices.why: Right: customers waiting now are what he acts on first.

choices.text: A pie of the month's deliveries by region
choices.why: True and about something else: it changes nothing at 11:00.

prompt: An operational screen leads with the ___ — the rows that are wrong, sorted by how wrong — and shrinks what is fine to a line.
hint: Not averages.

prompt: Three routes are 30 or more minutes behind. Route 6 has 23 stops planned and 5 done, route 10 has 22 planned and 5 done, route 11 has 25 planned and 3 done. By the board's definition, how many orders are at risk?
hint: At risk: not yet delivered, on a route 30 or more minutes behind.

prompt: The fourteen delays at 11:00 were 0, 6, 12, 18, 3, 35, 9, 22, 0, 41, 74, 15, 27 and 8 minutes. How many alerts would a threshold of 20 minutes have raised, counting a route that reaches the threshold?
hint: Put 20 in a fourth threshold column of your sheet.

prompt: At a 15-minute threshold, seven of fourteen routes alert at 11:00. What is the lesson's objection?
hint: What does a person learn from a phone that buzzes for nothing?

choices.text: Fifteen minutes is shorter than the copy interval, so the alerts would be stale
choices.why: The copy runs every ten minutes, which is shorter than fifteen.

choices.text: It would miss route 11, the one that matters most
choices.why: Route 11, at 74 minutes, alerts at every threshold in the table.

choices.text: Marcos learns to ignore the buzzing
choices.why: Right: alarm fatigue. An alert that fires too often is a switched-off alert.

choices.text: The IF formula cannot compare a delay with a threshold below 30
choices.why: The same formula counted 7 at 15 in your sheet.

prompt: A 60-minute threshold raises one alert that morning, for route 11. Why is that not the cautious choice it looks like?
hint: What has already happened to a route an hour behind?

choices.text: One alert a day is too few for anyone to trust the board
choices.why: Trust is not measured by the number of alerts; what the alert lets him change is.

choices.text: By then the route's windows are lost, so the alert reports a failure
choices.why: Right: three customers had already missed their window when route 11 crossed 60.

choices.text: Sixty minutes is the statistical rule for an outlier in delivery data, which makes it too strict for a warehouse
choices.why: There is no such rule; the threshold is a business decision, not a statistical result.

choices.text: It would fire every ten minutes for the rest of the day
choices.why: The once-per-crossing rule prevents that at any threshold; it is not the problem with 60.

prompt: Put in order the way Lívia and Marcos chose and kept the alert threshold.
hint: Count before choosing, and review after.
items: Count the alerts each would have raised on a real day
Ask which of those alerts Marcos could still have acted on
Count each month how many alerts led to an action
trap: Agreeing a line first and counting afterwards is the tempting order, and it turns the count into a justification instead of a test.

prompt: Which of these messages is an alert in the lesson's sense, not a notification?
hint: Who should do what, now, with which data?

choices.text: Route 11 is 74 minutes behind.
choices.why: A fact with no action: Marcos is left to work out what it means.

choices.text: Average delay across the whole fleet is now 19.3 minutes, above the 15-minute target.
choices.why: An alert on an average says nothing about where to act.

choices.text: Route 11: 22 stops left, 3 windows missed; route 14 is next door: move 6 stops?
choices.why: Right: it names the action and carries the data needed to take it.

choices.text: Deliveries are late today. Please check the board when you have a moment and act as needed.
choices.why: Polite and empty: no route, no action, no data.

prompt: About an alert, the number to keep is not how many fired, but how many led to an ___.
hint: Marcos doing something.

prompt: The pipeline copied its last data at 09:20, and nobody noticed until a customer rang at 11:05. For how many minutes did the board show an old picture as current?
When the copy stopped at 09:20, why did the board look calm rather than broken?
hint: What did the routes look like at 09:20?

choices.text: The pipeline raised an error, and the board hid it from Marcos
choices.why: The pipeline raised nothing: from its side there was simply nothing new to copy.

choices.text: Nobody was behind at 09:20, and with no new data no route could fall behind
choices.why: Right: a frozen board shows the last picture it had, and that picture was calm.

choices.text: Tiago had switched the alerts off for maintenance that morning
choices.why: The lesson says nothing of the kind; the alerts had no new delays to fire on.

choices.text: The board showed an average of the delays, which hid route 11 behind the others
choices.why: The board lists exceptions; at 09:20 there were none to list.

prompt: The data is copied every 10 minutes, and the board hides its numbers after 20 minutes without a copy. What is the reasoning behind 20?
hint: How many missed copies make a failure?

choices.text: Twenty minutes is how long a pipeline needs to restart on its own
choices.why: The lesson gives no restart time; 20 is a count of missed copies.

choices.text: Marcos looks at the board once every twenty minutes
choices.why: He acts every fifteen to thirty minutes, and the rule is about the copies, not his habits.

choices.text: It matches the 15-minute alert threshold rounded up to a round number
choices.why: The alert threshold is 30 minutes of delay, a different thing from the age of the data.

choices.text: One missed copy is a hiccup; two in a row is a failure
choices.why: Right: twice the interval separates a late copy from a stopped one.

prompt: How fresh does the data on Marcos's board need to be, by the lesson's argument?
hint: Lesson 2, the value of information, applied to time.

choices.text: Seconds old, because newer data is worth more to any decision
choices.why: Newer data is worth paying for only if somebody would act differently because of it.

choices.text: Fresh enough for his rhythm: he acts every 15 to 30 minutes, so a 10-minute copy will do
choices.why: Right: the rhythm of the decision sets the freshness.

choices.text: Yesterday's data, like the monthly review
choices.why: Yesterday serves a monthly decision; trucks move in minutes.

choices.text: An hour old, so that each copy is complete
choices.why: An hour-old picture moves stops onto a truck that is no longer ahead.

prompt: Bruno wants a screen on the Contagem store floor for his staff. Which first draft follows this lesson?
hint: Same level as Marcos's board, different floor.

choices.text: This year's monthly sales against last year's, as two lines
choices.why: A tactical comparison: it changes nothing on the floor this afternoon.

choices.text: The store's average days of stock, refreshed every ten minutes
choices.why: A monthly measure refreshed more often is the wrong picture the lesson names first.

choices.text: What is empty on the shelf now, best sellers first
choices.why: Right: the exceptions, sorted by what matters to the store; the time of the data goes in its header.

choices.text: The nine stores ranked by their sales per square metre
choices.why: A strategic comparison between stores; the staff cannot act on it today.

prompt: Customer service wants an alert when callers wait too long. Last Monday, a 2-minute wait would have fired 140 times, a 5-minute wait 12 times and a 15-minute wait once, at closing. What should Lívia do next?
hint: The threshold is chosen with the person who pays both costs.

choices.text: Ask the supervisor which of the 12 she could have acted on, and choose with her
choices.why: Right: count, then decide with the person who receives the alerts.

choices.text: Choose 2 minutes, because more alerts mean fewer callers left waiting on the line
choices.why: 140 alerts a day is alarm fatigue; the ones that matter get lost.

choices.text: Choose 15 minutes, since one alert a day is easy to handle
choices.why: One alert at closing reports a failure nobody can still fix.

choices.text: Alert on the average wait for the day instead
choices.why: An average says nothing about which caller is waiting now.

prompt: Match each failure with the way it shows on an operational board.
hint: Two of them look like good news.

pairs.right: Numbers that stop changing, on a calm board
572 orders on a day planned for 286
Thirteen route chips where fourteen were expected
Alerts that end with nobody doing anything
